subject: English Literature
source: AQA GCSE English Literature 8702 specification, Paper 1 Section B (19th-century novel) from own knowledge; Drive material reviewed (a Christmas Carol key-words document exists but the English Literature scheme of work in Drive is Pearson International GCSE, so not adapted). Quotations are short fair-dealing extracts only.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: A Christmas Carol - Context and Stave 1
lessons.title: A Christmas Carol: Dickens, Victorian Britain and the exam
objectives: Describe Dickens's life and the Victorian context that shaped the novella
Explain how the AQA Paper 1 Section B question is marked
Identify Dickens's main purpose in writing the story

keywords.def: a story shorter than a novel but longer than a short story
a chapter of A Christmas Carol, named like a verse of a song
a Victorian institution where the poor were housed and made to work
the social, historical and personal background to a text

starter: Define 'theme' and give one theme from a novel or film you know.
What does it mean to 'analyse' a quotation?
In one sentence, why do writers write about social problems?

teach.heading: Charles Dickens and the novella
bullets: Published in December 1843 and very popular straight away
Dickens was born in 1812 and later became a famous novelist
As a boy of twelve, he worked in a blacking factory
His father was imprisoned for debt, which shaped his sympathies
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Explain that Dickens knew poverty from childhood, so his sympathy is personal. Tell pupils the book has five staves, like songs in a carol. Note: Christmas is a Christian festival; we study the book as literature, and its themes of generosity and social responsibility connect with values we share.

teach.heading: Victorian poverty and the Poor Law
bullets: The Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834 made workhouses harsh
Many poor families, including children, worked long hours for little pay
Some wealthy people believed the poor were responsible for their poverty
Dickens wanted readers to see the poor as people
teach.note: Explain that workhouses were designed to be unpleasant so only the desperate would enter. Mention that Dickens was disturbed by reports about child labour in the early 1840s. Ask: if you wanted to change attitudes, why might a story work better than a pamphlet?

teach.heading: Dickens's purpose
bullets: To criticise greed and indifference to the poor
To show that people can change and be redeemed
To remind rich readers of their responsibility to others
To entertain: a ghost story with humour
teach.note: Ask pupils to rank the four purposes. Many will say the moral purpose; push them to see that the entertainment makes the moral message memorable. The subtitle calls it 'a ghost story of Christmas'. We analyse the ghosts as a literary device in a fictional story.

teach.heading: The Paper 1 Section B question
bullets: 30 marks, closed book
Starting with an extract, then the whole novel
AO1 response 12, AO2 language and structure 12, AO3 context 6
About 45 minutes in a 1 hour 45 exam
teach.note: Show a sample stem: 'Starting with this extract, explain how Dickens presents Scrooge. Write about how Dickens presents Scrooge in this extract and in the novel as a whole.' Stress that context (AO3) is woven in, not bolted on. Section B has no SPaG marks.

teach.heading: Making links to context
bullets: Link context to a specific quotation
Explain what Dickens wants the Victorian reader to think
Avoid long history lessons in the answer
Show that the message still matters today
teach.note: Practise a model sentence: 'Dickens presents Scrooge as cold and mean to criticise those Victorians who believed the poor deserved their poverty.' Notice it links idea, character and context in one sentence.

practice: Match each fact to its likely effect on how Dickens writes: (a) he worked in a factory at twelve; (b) workhouses were harsh; (c) the story is a ghost story.
Write one sentence explaining why Dickens chose a story rather than a speech to reach rich readers.
independent: Make a mind-map with Dickens in the centre and four branches: life, Victorian society, purpose, exam question.
Write two sentences linking context to meaning, starting 'Dickens wants Victorian readers to...'.
Write three questions you want to answer as we read the novella.
exit: Name one fact about Dickens's life and one about Victorian poverty.
State what AO3 means in the Section B question.
lessons.homework: Read Stave 1 up to Scrooge's reply to the charity gentlemen, and write down three words or phrases that describe Scrooge.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a timeline with images and a simplified glossary (workhouse, debt, factory). Stretch: research and explain one example of a Victorian reformer or charity and how it compares with Dickens's message.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: A Christmas Carol - Context and Stave 1
lessons.title: Stave 1: presenting Scrooge as a miser
objectives: Analyse how Dickens introduces Scrooge in Stave 1
Zoom in on key words and images of coldness and isolation
Link Scrooge's attitudes to Victorian context

keywords.def: a person who hoards money and spends as little as possible
a comparison using 'like' or 'as'
a series of words or phrases for emphasis
weather or setting that reflects mood

starter: Name one thing Dickens wanted to criticise in Victorian society.
What is the Poor Law?
Define 'AO2' in your own words.

teach.heading: Scrooge introduced
bullets: Dickens opens with 'Marley was dead: to begin with.'
Then Scrooge is described through a string of harsh adjectives
He is 'a squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching' sinner
The listing builds a picture of greed
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Read the list aloud with a harsh voice. Ask: what do all these verbs have in common? Elicit hands, grabbing, taking. The list is also quick and relentless, mimicking his hunger for money.

teach.heading: Coldness and isolation
bullets: He is described as 'hard and sharp as flint'
He is 'solitary as an oyster'
Cold weather does not affect him: he carries his own cold
These images show him closed, hard and alone
teach.note: Focus on similes. Flint is hard, strikes sparks, cold; oyster is closed shell, hidden, solitary. Ask what these images suggest about his heart and relationships. Link to AO2: simile, connotation, effect on the reader.

teach.heading: Scrooge's words reveal him
bullets: 'Bah! Humbug!' dismisses joy and kindness
'Are there no prisons?' shows contempt for the poor
He wants the poor to 'decrease the surplus population'
Rhetorical questions show he thinks he is above them
teach.note: Ask: how might a Victorian reader respond? Some wealthy readers shared such views; Dickens exposes how cruel they sound. Mention that the phrase 'surplus population' echoes ideas associated with Malthus. Discuss: do we only judge Scrooge by what he says?

teach.heading: Fred, Bob and the charity men
bullets: Fred offers warmth; Scrooge replies coldly
Bob Cratchit works in a freezing office with a tiny fire
The charity gentlemen ask Scrooge to help the poor
Dickens contrasts generosity and meanness
teach.note: Contrasts help characterisation. Ask pupils how each person shows what Scrooge lacks. Remind them that in the exam, using the whole novel means referring to different moments, not retelling the plot.

teach.heading: Write about Scrooge
bullets: Point: Dickens presents Scrooge as cold and isolated
Evidence: 'solitary as an oyster'
Analysis: the simile suggests a closed, protective shell
Context: Dickens criticises the isolation caused by greed
teach.note: Model the full paragraph on screen with each element coloured. Emphasise the final link to context in a single sentence.

practice: Explain what the simile 'hard and sharp as flint' suggests about Scrooge's character.
Choose two verbs from the list 'squeezing, wrenching, grasping' and explain the connotations.
independent: Write a PEAL paragraph (Point, Evidence, Analysis, Link to context) on 'solitary as an oyster'.
Write a second paragraph on Scrooge's reply 'Are there no prisons?' linking to the Poor Law.
Choose two quotations about Scrooge that you will learn by heart for the closed-book exam.
exit: Give one quotation from Stave 1 and say what it shows about Scrooge.
Name one technique and its effect in Dickens's description of Scrooge.
lessons.homework: Learn two short quotations about Scrooge from Stave 1 and write a paragraph on one of them, adding a context link.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a quotation bank with images and a paragraph scaffold. Stretch: evaluate whether Dickens expects the reader to hate Scrooge or pity him at this point.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: A Christmas Carol - Context and Stave 1
lessons.title: Stave 1: Marley's ghost and the supernatural
objectives: Explain the function of Marley's ghost in the plot and theme
Analyse Gothic features and symbols such as chains
Link Marley's warning to the idea of social responsibility

keywords.def: a style of writing using dark, eerie settings and supernatural events
an object or image that stands for a bigger idea
hinting at later events
being saved from a bad or sinful state

starter: Give two quotations that describe Scrooge.
What does a simile do?
Why does the novella begin with Marley's death?

teach.heading: Why a ghost?
bullets: Marley appears to warn Scrooge about his future
He is a ghost story device that drives the plot
He shows the cost of a selfish life
He introduces the three spirits to come
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Remind pupils that the ghost is a fictional device in a moral story; we analyse what Dickens does with it. Ask: what would be lost if Scrooge simply changed his mind on his own?

teach.heading: Gothic atmosphere
bullets: The door-knocker transforms into Marley's face
Bells ring and a clanking of chains is heard
The setting is dark, cold and foggy
Dickens builds fear before Marley even appears
teach.note: Focus on the sequence of eerie details. Ask pupils which senses are used (sound, sight, touch). This is the 'build and release' structure of a ghost story and it prepares the reader to believe in the supernatural.

teach.heading: The chain as symbol
bullets: Marley says: 'I wear the chain I forged in life'
He made it 'link by link, and yard by yard'
It is made of cash-boxes, keys and ledgers
Scrooge's own chain is longer, Marley warns
teach.note: Ask pupils to explain the symbol: chain as burden of choices; the repetition in 'link by link, and yard by yard' shows the slow accumulation of selfish acts. The idea of forging suggests Marley made his own punishment, a theme of personal responsibility.

teach.heading: Marley's regret and message
bullets: Marley cries: 'Mankind was my business'
He regrets ignoring the poor and suffering
He says he cannot rest or share comfort
His warning shows what lies ahead for Scrooge
teach.note: Connect to social responsibility. Dickens argues that everyone is responsible for the welfare of others. This echoes the Islamic emphasis on the rights of the poor and needy, for example in Surah al-Ma'un (107), which criticises those who do not urge the feeding of the needy. Keep the focus on the text.

teach.heading: Linking to the whole novel
bullets: Marley's visit sets up the structure of the story
Scrooge reacts with disbelief and humour, then fear
His denial ('a bit of undigested beef') shows his scepticism
Fear is the first step towards change
teach.note: Ask pupils how Scrooge's attitude to the supernatural reveals his character. For Q8-style answers, encourage pupils to jump from this moment to later ones: the other spirits as fuller versions of Marley's warning.

practice: Explain what the chain symbolises in one sentence.
Pick one Gothic detail from Marley's arrival and explain the effect on the reader.
independent: Write a PEAL paragraph on 'I wear the chain I forged in life' including a link to context or theme.
Write a second paragraph on 'Mankind was my business' linking to the theme of responsibility.
Complete a table of three Gothic features, their effects and one quotation for each.
exit: Name one effect Dickens creates through Marley's chains.
lessons.homework: Learn the quotation 'I wear the chain I forged in life' and write a paragraph explaining its meaning and effect.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide visual prompts for Gothic imagery and a model paragraph. Stretch: compare Marley's regret with the regrets Scrooge will face later.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: A Christmas Carol - The Spirits and redemption
lessons.title: Stave 2: the Ghost of Christmas Past
objectives: Explain how memory shows Scrooge's past and the roots of his coldness
Analyse the contrast between Fezziwig and Scrooge
Understand Belle's role in Scrooge's loss

keywords.def: a longing for the happy past
a clear difference between two things
something that is loved or worshipped too much
feeling sorry for someone else's suffering

starter: Give one Gothic feature in Marley's visit.
Explain what 'link by link' suggests.
What is the purpose of the Ghost of Christmas Past in the story?

teach.heading: A strange spirit
bullets: The Ghost looks like both a child and an old man
A bright light shines from the top of its head
It carries a cap that can put out the light
The light suggests memory and truth
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask: why would Dickens make the spirit both young and old? Elicit that memory links old and young self. The light could symbolise truth or illumination, but note that the cap shows Scrooge wants to hide from it.

teach.heading: A lonely boy
bullets: Scrooge sees himself as 'a solitary child' at school
He weeps for neglect and loneliness
Dickens invites sympathy for Scrooge
His coldness has a cause, not just a nature
teach.note: Link to Dickens's own childhood experience of abandonment. Ask: does understanding why someone becomes selfish change how you judge them? This can move the discussion towards compassion without excusing cruelty.

teach.heading: Fezziwig's party
bullets: Fezziwig throws a joyful Christmas ball for his workers
A small expense creates great happiness
Scrooge speaks warmly about his old master
He realises how he treats Bob
teach.note: Compare Fezziwig as the model of a kind employer with Scrooge as the opposite. Fezziwig shows that wealth can be used for others. Ask pupils to find the moment Scrooge recognises his own failings: he thinks of his clerk.

teach.heading: Belle and the 'golden idol'
bullets: Belle ends their engagement because money has replaced love
She says another idol has displaced her, 'a golden one'
Scrooge pleads that she has misjudged him
He loses love by choosing wealth
teach.note: An idol is something worshipped; Belle accuses him of valuing gold above people. Dickens warns that greed destroys relationships. Ask pupils to compare her gentleness with his defensiveness.

teach.heading: Exam link
bullets: Use Stave 2 to show why Scrooge is not simply evil
Contrast young and old Scrooge
Link memory to the theme of redemption
Quote briefly and analyse precisely
teach.note: Practise a paragraph that moves from extract to the novel: 'Even before Scrooge meets the spirit, Dickens presents him as hard; however, in Stave 2 the image of the solitary child encourages sympathy, which suggests change is possible.'

practice: Explain what 'a solitary child' suggests about young Scrooge.
Why does Dickens include Fezziwig's party?
independent: Write a PEAL paragraph about Belle's words 'another idol has displaced me' and link to context.
Write a paragraph comparing Fezziwig with Scrooge as employers.
Choose one quotation from Stave 2 to learn by heart and annotate it.
exit: Name one reason Dickens makes us feel sympathy for Scrooge in Stave 2.
What do Fezziwig and Belle each show about Scrooge?
lessons.homework: Write a short paragraph answering: 'How does Dickens use the past to explain Scrooge?' Include two quotations.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a comparison table (Fezziwig/Scrooge) and sentence stems. Stretch: argue whether Scrooge is a victim of his past or responsible for his choices.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: A Christmas Carol - The Spirits and redemption
lessons.title: Stave 3: the Ghost of Christmas Present, the Cratchits and Ignorance and Want
objectives: Analyse how Dickens presents the Cratchit family
Explain the symbolism of Ignorance and Want
Link Tiny Tim and the Cratchits to Dickens's message

keywords.def: using objects or characters to represent ideas
a quality that arouses pity or sadness
a message that tells someone about possible danger
a horn overflowing with food, symbolising abundance

starter: Name one quotation about young Scrooge.
What does 'idol' mean in Belle's speech?
How would you describe Fezziwig's attitude to his workers?

teach.heading: A spirit of generosity
bullets: The Ghost of Christmas Present is large, jolly and green-robed
He sits among food, drink and plenty
He is generous and warm, yet firm with Scrooge
Dickens contrasts him with Scrooge's meanness
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask pupils to picture the scene: piles of food, bright fire, holly, a generous host. The spirit stands for joy and abundance, which are available to all if shared.

teach.heading: The Cratchit household
bullets: Bob earns only fifteen shillings a week
Mrs Cratchit and the children enjoy a small Christmas dinner
They are grateful and happy with what they have
Dickens shows love, not wealth, makes a home rich
teach.note: Ask: how does Dickens avoid presenting the poor as pitiful? He shows dignity, love and gratitude. Mention the modest pudding that seems a triumph to the family. Link to Scrooge's own lonely wealth.

teach.heading: Tiny Tim and pathos
bullets: Tiny Tim is small, ill and uses a crutch
He says 'God bless Us, Every One!'
Scrooge asks if Tim will live
The spirit throws Scrooge's own words back at him
teach.note: Pathos aims to move readers. Tiny Tim makes the abstract problem of poverty personal. When the spirit repeats Scrooge's phrase about the 'surplus population', Scrooge is shamed. Ask pupils what makes this moment powerful.

teach.heading: Ignorance and Want
bullets: Two children appear beneath the spirit's robe
They are 'yellow, meagre, ragged, scowling, wolfish'
The boy is Ignorance and the girl is Want
Dickens warns of 'Doom' unless society changes
teach.note: Link this to the Victorian debate on education and poverty. Dickens suggests that neglect creates danger for everyone. Notice the animal-like adjective 'wolfish' and the listing of grim adjectives. Ask: why does Dickens save this image for late in the Stave?

teach.heading: Fred's party
bullets: Fred's household laughs and plays games
They toast Scrooge despite his coldness
Scrooge begins to join in unseen
Dickens shows joy is shared and spreading
teach.note: Briefly compare Fred and Scrooge. Fred offers forgiveness. Scrooge is moved but not yet changed. Ask what the games and laughter suggest about community.

practice: Explain in one sentence why Dickens makes the Cratchits grateful rather than bitter.
Explain what 'Ignorance' and 'Want' might stand for in Victorian society.
independent: Write a PEAL paragraph on Ignorance and Want, using one short quotation and a link to context.
Write a paragraph on Tiny Tim and how Dickens creates pathos.
Complete a comparison table of the Cratchits and Scrooge: home, money, relationships, attitudes.
exit: Name two things the Cratchit family show Scrooge.
What is the effect of Ignorance and Want being children?
lessons.homework: Learn the quotation about Ignorance and Want and write a paragraph answering: 'How does Dickens present poverty in Stave 3?'
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide images of Victorian homes and a glossary of terms. Stretch: evaluate whether Dickens romanticises the poor and justify your view.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: A Christmas Carol - The Spirits and redemption
lessons.title: Stave 4: the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
objectives: Analyse how Dickens creates fear and dread through the final spirit
Explain the effect of the scenes about Scrooge's death
Link Tiny Tim's fate and the grave to the idea of choice

keywords.def: suggesting that something bad will happen
absence of speech, used here to build fear
a result of an action
the fact that all humans must die

starter: What do Ignorance and Want represent?
Give a quotation from Tiny Tim.
Explain what 'pathos' means.

teach.heading: A silent, shrouded figure
bullets: The spirit is 'shrouded in a deep black garment'
Only a hand is visible
It does not speak, only points
Silence makes Scrooge more afraid
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask pupils why Dickens makes this spirit silent when the others talk. Elicit that silence is unsettling and leaves Scrooge to imagine the worst. The black garment suggests death and mystery.

teach.heading: Scrooge's death is ignored
bullets: Businessmen discuss his death casually
Thieves sell his belongings
Nobody mourns him
Dickens shows an unloved, wasted life
teach.note: This shows the consequence of a life without kindness. The scene with the charwoman and the laundress is grimly comic and bitter. Ask: what does this suggest about wealth that is not shared?

teach.heading: The Cratchits grieve
bullets: Tiny Tim has died, and the family is mournful
Bob speaks lovingly of his son
The contrast with Scrooge's unmourned death is strong
Scrooge is moved to tears
teach.note: Link pathos to purpose: Dickens wants the reader to feel the cost of neglect. Point out the quiet, dignified tone of the Cratchit scene compared with the cynical conversation about Scrooge.

teach.heading: The grave and the plea
bullets: Scrooge sees his name on a neglected gravestone
He asks if these are 'shadows of the things that May be'
He cries: 'I am not the man I was'
The future is not fixed if he changes
teach.note: The key idea: Scrooge pleads that the future can change. Dickens gives hope. Ask what Scrooge's change from commanding to begging shows. Link to the theme of redemption through choice.

teach.heading: Writing about fear and choice
bullets: Link the silence and darkness to dread
Explain how consequence persuades Scrooge
Show how fear leads to change
Use brief quotations and clear analysis
teach.note: Model an exam link: 'By presenting a future where Scrooge dies alone, Dickens warns his readers that selfish lives are unmourned and wasted.' Ask pupils to improve it with a precise quotation and a context link.

practice: Explain in one sentence why Dickens makes the final spirit silent.
What does Scrooge's plea 'I am not the man I was' show about him?
independent: Write a PEAL paragraph on the description of the final spirit, including a quotation and an effect.
Write a paragraph comparing the reaction to Scrooge's death with the reaction to Tiny Tim's death.
Plan a four-point answer to the question: 'How does Dickens use fear in Stave 4?'
exit: Name one way Dickens creates fear in Stave 4.
What does the final spirit's warning teach Scrooge?
lessons.homework: Learn the quotation about 'shadows of the things that May be' and write a paragraph explaining its significance.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a sequence cards activity for the Stave 4 scenes. Stretch: evaluate whether fear or love is more effective in changing Scrooge.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: A Christmas Carol - The Spirits and redemption
lessons.title: Stave 5: redemption and the message of the novella
objectives: Analyse how Dickens presents Scrooge's transformation
Explain how language and structure create joy and hope
Evaluate Dickens's final message

keywords.def: a complete change in character or form
a sudden, emotional expression
three linked words or phrases for emphasis
the lesson or message of a story

starter: Give one reason the future spirit is silent.
What does 'redemption' mean?
Write a sentence linking fear to change.

teach.heading: A joyful waking
bullets: Scrooge wakes up and finds he is alive
He is 'as light as a feather' and 'as merry as a schoolboy'
He is excited by simple things like the bedposts and the sunlight
His changing language shows a new person
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Read the lines with growing energy. Ask pupils to note the similes and what is surprising about them: a stern old man acting like a boy. The repetition of 'I am as...' shows his giddiness.

teach.heading: Actions, not just words
bullets: He sends a prize turkey to the Cratchits
He gives to the charity gentlemen
He visits Fred and joins the party
He raises Bob's salary and helps his family
teach.note: Ask: why does Dickens show practical actions? Because redemption must be proved by deeds, not feelings. Link to the wider idea that real faith and goodness are shown in what we do for others.

teach.heading: Language of change
bullets: Scrooge says he will 'honour Christmas in my heart'
Exclamations and short sentences show energy
The narrator calls him 'as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man'
A triple structure marks his full transformation
teach.note: Point out the repeated structure 'as good a... as good a... as good a...' and how it echoes the earlier lists of negative adjectives. The narrator's praise is the opposite of the opening list.

teach.heading: Tiny Tim and the ending
bullets: Tiny Tim does not die
Scrooge becomes like a second father to him
The final line repeats 'God bless Us, Every One!'
A cyclical ending offers hope and community
teach.note: Ask: is this ending too sweet or earned? Encourage evidence-based debate. Mention Dickens's purpose: to convince readers that change is possible and urgent.

teach.heading: Evaluating the message
bullets: Redemption is open to anyone who chooses it
Wealth should serve people, not own them
Community matters more than isolation
The message still matters today
teach.note: Prepare pupils for a thematic Q: 'How does Dickens present change?' Tell them to track the arc: Stave 1 cold and closed; Stave 5 warm and open. Use a before-and-after chart.

practice: Compare the opening description of Scrooge with the narrator's final description. Name two changes.
Explain what the repeated 'as good a...' suggests.
independent: Write a PEAL paragraph on 'as light as a feather' showing how Dickens presents Scrooge's change.
Write a paragraph on the practical actions Scrooge takes and why they matter.
Complete a before-and-after chart for Scrooge: language, actions, relationships and attitudes.
exit: Name two ways Scrooge shows he has changed.
What is Dickens's message in the final stave?
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph evaluating whether Scrooge's transformation is believable, with two quotations.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide before-and-after pictures and a simple chart template. Stretch: connect Scrooge's transformation to ideas of repentance and amending one's behaviour in different traditions.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: A Christmas Carol - Writing the exam response
lessons.title: Writing a Section B response: extract and whole novel
objectives: Plan and write a full Section B response
Move smoothly from the extract to the novel as a whole
Assess your answer against assessment objectives

keywords.def: a short passage printed on the exam paper
your central argument in a response
woven into your own sentence
a reasoned conclusion supported by evidence

starter: Name three quotations you have learnt from the novella.
State what AO1, AO2 and AO3 each reward.
Which stave shows Scrooge's change?

teach.heading: Unpick the question
bullets: Typical stem: how does Dickens present Scrooge?
Part one: look closely at the extract
Part two: refer to the novel as a whole
Underline the key word: present, show, explore
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Display a sample question: 'Starting with this extract, explain how Dickens presents Scrooge's attitude to others. Write about how Dickens presents Scrooge in this extract and how Dickens presents Scrooge in the novel as a whole.' The extract is from Stave 1, the scene with the charity gentlemen; use your class edition of the text.

teach.heading: Plan in five minutes
bullets: Write a clear one-sentence argument
Choose two points from the extract
Choose two points from elsewhere in the novel
Add a context link to each point
teach.note: Model a plan: Thesis: Dickens presents Scrooge as isolated and unfeeling to criticise Victorian greed, but also shows he can change. Extract points: his words to the charity men; his abrupt manner. Novel points: Marley's warning; Stave 5 transformation.

teach.heading: Paragraph structure
bullets: Point linked to the question
Embedded quotation
Zoom in: word, technique, effect
Link to context or to the whole novel
teach.note: Model a paragraph and highlight each element in a different colour. Insist on explaining how language and structure create meaning, not just what a character does.

teach.heading: Linking across the novel
bullets: Use phrases like 'Later in the novella...'
Link moments rather than listing them
Show development, not just repeat a single idea
Use short quotations, not long ones
teach.note: Pupils often retell the plot. Teach them to link ideas: 'Dickens's presentation of Scrooge as cold in Stave 1 contrasts with his generosity in Stave 5, which shows that selfishness is a choice, not fate.'

teach.heading: Check against the mark scheme
bullets: AO1: a clear, personal argument with quotations
AO2: precise comments on language, form and structure
AO3: relevant context woven into the analysis
Time yourself: about 45 minutes in the exam
teach.note: Share a simplified mark scheme and ask pupils to check their plan against each AO. Emphasise: a short, focused answer beats a long unfocused one.

practice: Write a one-sentence thesis in answer to: 'How does Dickens present Scrooge's attitude to others?'
Write the first sentence of a paragraph that moves from the extract to the whole novel.
independent: Write a full answer (about 30 minutes) to: 'Starting with the extract from Stave 1 (Scrooge's reply to the charity gentlemen), explain how Dickens presents Scrooge's attitude to the poor in this extract and in the novel as a whole.'
Highlight your thesis, three quotations and two context links.
Write one target based on the AO checklist.
exit: State the two parts of the Section B question.
Name one technique you will use to link the extract to the novel.
lessons.homework: Redraft one paragraph of your answer, improving the analysis of a single word and adding a context link.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: allow a paragraph frame and a bank of learnt quotations; split the task across two sittings if needed. Stretch: add an evaluative sentence on how convincing Dickens's message is for a modern reader.
